flag_basis: Texas has a comparatively dense GoodLeap-specific court record involving residential solar financing, electronic contract formation, arbitration, installer conduct, Truth in Lending claims, and recent appellate decisions. Broader Texas solar enforcement and new state regulation are tracked separately and must not be described as GoodLeap-specific enforcement unless GoodLeap is actually named.
editorial_rule: Court holdings may be stated as holdings. Claims made by consumers or government plaintiffs must remain clearly labeled as allegations unless independently established. A ruling compelling arbitration is not a ruling on the merits of the underlying consumer allegations.

core_cases.holding: The court reversed a default judgment against GoodLeap because error was apparent in the service record and remanded for further proceedings.
core_cases.allegations_or_background: McGrew's underlying pro se suit arose from a 2021 residential solar loan and asserted fraud, forgery, contract, warranty, Texas DTPA, and unjust-enrichment claims. Those allegations were not resolved on the merits by the appellate decision.
core_cases.why_it_matters: Very recent Texas appellate decision involving GoodLeap. Useful for tracking litigation posture and demonstrating that not every GoodLeap appellate case is an arbitration ruling.

core_cases.case: GoodLeap, LLC v. Samuel Ramirez Garza
core_cases.holding: The appellate court reversed the trial court's denial of GoodLeap's motion to compel arbitration and remanded. The court concluded that, on the record before it, GoodLeap met its initial burden and Garza did not create a fact issue preventing enforcement of the arbitration agreement.
core_cases.allegations_or_background: Garza alleged that door-to-door salespeople made promises about eliminating his electric bill, a $7,000 payment, and a carport roof; that he did not understand he was entering a separate GoodLeap loan; and that the transaction documents and amounts differed. The opinion recounts those allegations but does not adjudicate their truth.
core_cases.why_it_matters: One of the strongest Texas sources for explaining how courts analyze electronic assent and arbitration in a door-to-door solar financing transaction.

core_cases.case: Solcius, LLC and GoodLeap, LLC (formerly Loanpal) v. Salvador Meraz
core_cases.holding: The court reversed the trial court's denial of the motion to compel arbitration, holding that the record contained conclusive evidence that Meraz electronically signed contracts containing arbitration provisions. It remanded with instructions to compel arbitration and stay the lawsuit.
core_cases.allegations_or_background: Meraz alleged that the installed system did not perform as represented, work at a second property was not completed, and roof damage occurred. He later disputed signing the electronic contracts. The appellate court's holding concerned arbitration and electronic execution, not the merits of the installation allegations.
core_cases.why_it_matters: Earlier Texas appellate precedent showing successful use of DocuSign evidence to establish electronic execution of solar and GoodLeap agreements.

core_cases.case: Donaciano Salinas Lopez and Imelda Hinojosa Lopez v. Meraki Solar, LLC, Solcius, LLC, Karla Trevino, and GoodLeap, LLC
core_cases.court: U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Texas, McAllen Division
core_cases.holding: The federal court denied GoodLeap's motion to compel arbitration without prejudice and ordered limited discovery on contract-formation issues. The consumers submitted sworn declarations saying they never signed the GoodLeap loan agreement; GoodLeap relied on its electronic records and DocuSign materials.
core_cases.allegations_or_background: The Lopezes alleged that a salesperson represented the system would fully power their home and eliminate the need to purchase electricity and that they were unaware of a separate financing agreement. The court did not decide the truth of those substantive sales allegations in this order.
core_cases.why_it_matters: Key counterpoint to Meraz and Garza: a Texas federal court found the formation dispute required development before arbitration could be compelled. This makes Texas particularly useful for a neutral consumer explainer on when signature disputes matter.
core_cases.source_tier: primary federal court opinion via GovInfo

core_cases.case: Alma Ramos and Indara Ramos v. GoodLeap, LLC, et al.
core_cases.court: U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Texas
core_cases.holding: On June 2, 2025, the court granted GoodLeap's motion to compel arbitration and stayed the case after the plaintiffs filed a statement of non-opposition to the motion.
core_cases.allegations_or_background: The docket categorizes the matter as a Truth in Lending case. Complaint-level allegations should not be summarized editorially until the complaint itself is reviewed.
core_cases.why_it_matters: Recent federal example where arbitration was granted without the contested formation analysis seen in Lopez.

core_cases.case: Kassandra Elejarza v. GoodLeap, LLC, et al.
core_cases.court: U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Texas
core_cases.holding: At a July 15, 2025 motion hearing, the court granted motions to compel arbitration, stayed the case, and administratively closed it.
core_cases.allegations_or_background: The federal docket identifies the case as a Truth in Lending matter. Complaint allegations require separate primary-document review before publication.
core_cases.why_it_matters: Adds to the recent concentration of GoodLeap arbitration litigation in the Southern District of Texas and links the financing dispute to TriSMART Solar.

secondary_case_leads.status_at_last_verified_docket: GoodLeap filed a motion to compel arbitration on September 3, 2025; later docket materials show arbitration briefing. Do not state an outcome until a later order is verified.

texas_regulatory_context.title: Texas Attorney General solar fraud initiative
texas_regulatory_context.scope: broader Texas solar market; not GoodLeap-specific
texas_regulatory_context.verified_fact: The Texas Attorney General announced a solar-fraud initiative and said it had issued civil investigative demands to several solar companies after receiving more than 100 complaints concerning the named companies collectively. The announcement names Freedom Forever, Sunrun, Lone Star Solar Services, and CAM Solar; it does not name GoodLeap.
texas_regulatory_context.editorial_use: Useful context for the Texas solar enforcement environment. Never phrase this as an investigation of GoodLeap based on the cited release.

texas_regulatory_context.title: Texas AG lawsuit against CAM Solar
texas_regulatory_context.scope: broader Texas solar market; not GoodLeap-specific
texas_regulatory_context.verified_fact: The Texas Attorney General sued CAM Solar alleging fraudulent and deceptive practices in solar-panel sales. The action followed the broader April 2026 initiative.
texas_regulatory_context.editorial_use: Demonstrates active Texas solar enforcement, but should remain clearly separated from GoodLeap-specific litigation.

texas_regulatory_context.title: Texas Residential Solar Retailer Regulatory Act / TDLR program
texas_regulatory_context.scope: consumer protection and solar retail regulation
texas_regulatory_context.verified_fact: Texas began requiring specified residential-solar contract provisions and a five-business-day cancellation right for covered transactions on September 1, 2025. Beginning September 1, 2026, covered residential solar retailers and salespersons must be registered with TDLR. TDLR also states that where a covered solar sale or lease involves an affiliated or referred third-party lender, the agreement must require the lender to cancel an accompanying loan when the solar agreement is properly cancelled.
texas_regulatory_context.editorial_use: High-value official consumer resource for current Texas transactions. Because the registration mandate begins September 1, 2026, copy published before that date must describe it as upcoming rather than already effective.

texas_regulatory_context.title: Texas SB 1036 legislative record
texas_regulatory_context.scope: statutory basis for residential solar regulation
texas_regulatory_context.verified_fact: SB 1036 created the registration framework for residential solar retailers and salespersons and directed development of consumer educational materials regarding rights and remedies in residential solar transactions.
texas_regulatory_context.editorial_use: Use when explaining the source of the new TDLR framework or linking to statutory history.

page_storylines_supported_by_sources.note: Texas records include multiple orders compelling arbitration, but Lopez shows that a sworn dispute over whether consumers actually formed the GoodLeap agreement can require discovery before arbitration is decided.
